title: Team Sizes
statement:
A company has **n** employees numbered from 1 to n. Employee 1 is the CEO and has no boss. Every other employee i has exactly one direct boss p[i], and following bosses upwards from anyone always ends at the CEO, so the company is a tree rooted at employee 1.

The **team** of an employee consists of that employee and everyone below them (their direct reports, the reports of those, and so on). For every employee, print the size of their team.
input:
The first line contains an integer **n**.

The second line contains n - 1 integers p[2], p[3], ..., p[n]: the boss of employee 2, 3, ..., n. (When n = 1 this line is empty.) Note that a boss can have a larger number than the employee.
output: Print n integers on one line: the team sizes of employees 1, 2, ..., n.
constraints: the bosses form a tree rooted at 1

samples.explanation: Employee 2 leads 4 and 5, so the team of 2 has 3 people. Employee 3 leads 6.

hints: Store for every employee the list of their direct reports (children).
size(v) = 1 + the sum of size(c) over all children c. Compute it with DFS, or with a BFS order processed backwards.
The tree can be a long chain of 2·10^5 people: deep recursion may crash (especially in Python or Java). An iterative order avoids that.
editorial:
Build children lists from the parent array. Get an order of the vertices in which every parent comes before its children (a BFS from the root: start with [1] and append the children of each processed vertex). Then go through this order **backwards** and add `size[v]` to `size[parent[v]]`, starting from `size[v] = 1` for all v. When v is processed, all its descendants are already done. This avoids recursion, which is important for a chain-shaped tree.

Complexity: O(n).
